title: KHILADI — Beyond the Scoreboard
source: User-supplied completed SupeRR Selector methodology; figures not independently recomputed from raw data.
website: Deferred by user; no invented website footage.

scenes.caption: My first IPL team.
scenes.narration: In school, the back of my notebook had an IPL team. The front had mathematics. The team got considerably more attention.

scenes.caption: Then came the hackathon.
scenes.narration: Years later, the Rajasthan Royals hackathon brought that notebook back. This time, I wanted evidence. Who actually performs when the game gets difficult?

scenes.caption: 200,999 events. First: clean.
scenes.narration: First obstacle: two hundred thousand delivery events. Wides. No-balls. Run-outs. Rain. Before judging a player, I had to reconstruct the match correctly.

scenes.caption: Judge the situation BEFORE the ball.
scenes.narration: Then I froze time before every ball. Score. Wickets. Balls remaining. No peeking at the six that happened next. That would be cheating, with a spreadsheet.

scenes.caption: Difficult ≠ consequential.
scenes.narration: But difficult doesn't always mean consequential. Thirty-nine runs an over? Terrifying. Also, probably over. Two needed off one? Now the next ball can change everything.

scenes.caption: Difficulty + win-probability leverage.
scenes.narration: So I combined scoreboard difficulty with win-probability leverage, using context-relative percentiles. The primary definition selected the top twenty percent within each innings.

scenes.caption: Performance against expectation.
scenes.narration: Next question: better than what? I estimated expected runs and dismissal risk. Batters earned credit for extra runs and survival. Bowlers, for runs prevented and credited wickets.

scenes.caption: Context. Era. Opposition.
scenes.narration: I adjusted for scoring eras and opposition. Then combined runs and wickets with a declared assumption: fifteen runs per wicket. And checked ten and twenty too.

scenes.caption: Small sample? Shrink the claim.
scenes.narration: Then the small samples arrived, wearing enormous confidence. Twenty-five pressure events are not four hundred. Empirical Bayes pulled weakly supported estimates toward the average.

scenes.caption: Pressure quality ≠ pressure delta.
scenes.narration: And performing well under pressure isn't the same as improving because of pressure. Bowling showed no validated repeatable pressure delta. The batting delta gains were tiny.

scenes.caption: The holdout challenged the story.
scenes.narration: The unseen twenty-twenty-six season challenged my story. Batting quality showed no positive predictive relationship. Bowling looked promising, but an advantage over ordinary economy wasn't established.

scenes.caption: 750 match bootstraps.
scenes.narration: So I resampled whole matches, seven hundred and fifty times. Confidence intervals. Rank distributions. A top-ten bootstrap rate measures historical stability. It isn't a prophecy.

scenes.caption: Change assumptions. Watch ranks move.
scenes.narration: Change the pressure definition, and the shortlist changes. Remove a player's best season, and nine names leave each top ten. Those weren't details to hide.

scenes.caption: A shortlist, with evidence attached.
scenes.narration: The primary lists put Jos Buttler and Jasprit Bumrah first. But every name needs its exposure, uncertainty and format mix. T-twenty international evidence isn't automatically IPL evidence.

scenes.caption: 20 / 20 rankings reproduced.
scenes.narration: Finally, the replay reproduced all twenty rankings and passed forty-one checks. The code repeated. The statistical limitations stayed.

scenes.caption: Better questions. Honest answers.
scenes.narration: That notebook used to ask, who would I pick? Khiladi asks a better question. What does the evidence support... and how sure should I be?
